title: Exchange-controlled quantum beats and entanglement in an exciton--bimodal-cavity system
authors: Cesar E. P. Villegas, Victor P. Brasil, Pedro A. S. Contri, Kevin Lizárraga, Jonas Maziero
abstract: We theoretically demonstrate tunable population transfer and entanglement generation in a two-exciton system coupled to a bimodal optical cavity, including an exciton-exciton exchange interaction. By using dressed-state transformations and Löwdin partitioning, we derive effective Hamiltonians that identify three dynamical time scales: local polaritonic oscillations, long-period dressed-state beats, and direct excitonic exchange. We apply the framework to graphene nanoribbon excitons, using excitonic energies, transition dipoles, and lifetimes obtained from first-principles calculations to parameterize the model. In the small- and moderate-exchange regimes, the dynamics become multiscale, and the beat channel sustains sizable quantum entanglement over long dissipative time windows. In the large-exchange regime, the excitonic Hamiltonian dominates and drives nearly complete population transfer between excitonic states over many coherent cycles. The resulting analytical expressions provide direct design rules connecting the beat period, transfer amplitude, and coherent-cycle number to the exchange interaction, cavity detuning, and light--matter coupling. Our results establish a controllable route for engineering long-lived entanglement and coherent excitonic operations in exciton--bimodal-cavity systems.
summary: This theoretical study explores controlling quantum dynamics and entanglement in an exciton-bimodal-cavity system by leveraging an exciton-exciton exchange interaction. By deriving effective Hamiltonians for different energy regimes, the authors show how to engineer long-lived quantum correlations and achieve near-complete population transfer. The results provide direct design rules for realizing coherent excitonic operations in nanoscale platforms.
main_problem: The paper aims to demonstrate tunable population transfer and entanglement generation in a two-exciton system coupled to a bimodal optical cavity, incorporating an exciton-exciton exchange interaction.
main_result: The study establishes a controllable route for engineering long-lived entanglement and coherent excitonic operations by controlling the exchange interaction, cavity detuning, and light-matter coupling.
method: The authors use dressed-state transformations and Löwdin partitioning to derive effective Hamiltonians, solving the dynamics via the Lindblad master equation.
model_or_system: The system is a two-exciton system coupled to a bimodal optical cavity, modeled using a full Hamiltonian that includes exciton energies, cavity frequencies, coupling strengths, and an exchange interaction term. The analysis is applied to graphene nanoribbon excitons.
key_observables: Population transfer, entanglement concurrence, beat period, and excitonic coherent-cycle number.
important_parameters: Exchange interaction strength (J), cavity detuning, and light-matter coupling strength (g). The dynamics are analyzed in small/moderate and large-exchange regimes.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the use of the rotating-wave approximation and often focuses on the single-excitation subspace or specific energy regimes for simplification.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the system schematic, show population and entanglement dynamics for varying exchange interactions (small vs. large J), and present engineering maps relating beat period, transfer amplitude, and coherent cycles to control parameters.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by defining the full Hamiltonian and dynamics, then systematically decomposing the problem into effective Hamiltonians for different physical regimes (excitonic, local polaritonic, beat-polaritonic) using advanced mathematical techniques before deriving control rules.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant to AMO physics and quantum optics as it deals with cavity QED, engineered quantum dynamics, and the control of entanglement in solid-state excitonic systems.
